title: Time as a circle
hookLine: many churches walk the life of Christ every year, with colors and seasons

lines: A CLOCK FROM THE BACK ROW.
cards: Sit in the same church once a month for a year and watch the cloth on the altar. Late November, it turns purple, or in some churches deep blue. At Christmas, white and gold.
Then green for a while. Toward spring, purple again, for weeks. At Easter, white, bursting with lilies.
One Sunday in late spring, everything is suddenly red. Then green for months, all through summer and fall. Nobody announces it.
It's just there, like leaves changing on a tree outside the window. Those colors are a clock you can see from the back row. Today's word is the name of the whole circle.

teach.b: The liturgical year. Liturgy comes from the Greek leitourgia, a public work or service, often explained as the work of the people. It's the church's calendar, and it doesn't count money or school terms.

teach.h: A YEAR THROUGH THE LIFE OF JESUS.
teach.b: It walks through the life of Jesus, every year. In the Western churches it begins with Advent: four weeks of waiting in the dark before Christmas. Then Christmas, the birth.
Epiphany, God shown to the world. Lent, forty days in the desert. Holy Week, the cross, and Easter, the empty tomb.
Pentecost, the Spirit, fifty days later. Then the long green stretch the church calls ordinary time. Easter moves every year, because it follows the moon; Christmas stays put.
The Orthodox year starts on the first of September, and runs its own rhythm of feasts and fasts.
Ecclesiastes says: "To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven."

teach.h: TIME AS A LINE, AND A CIRCLE.
teach.b: Daily life runs on time as a line: deadlines, birthdays, one year after another. The church year makes time a circle too. You come back to the same stories every year, a different person each time.
The birth sounds different the year you have a baby. The cross sounds different the year you lose someone.
Catholics, Orthodox, Anglicans and Lutherans keep the full year, as do many Methodists and Presbyterians; many Baptist, evangelical and Pentecostal churches mark mainly Christmas and Easter.
For those who keep it, the circle makes the calendar itself holy.

how: Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican, Lutheran and many Methodist and Presbyterian churches follow the liturgical year, changing colors, readings and prayers with each season; many other churches celebrate mainly Christmas and Easter.

games.q: which season is which — tap the pairs.

s: the church year starts on January 1
in the Western churches it starts with Advent, in late November or early December. the Orthodox year starts on September 1.
Easter's date moves, but Christmas stays put
Easter follows the moon. Christmas is fixed on December 25 (though some churches reckon it by the old calendar).
every church keeps the full liturgical year
many Baptist, evangelical and Pentecostal churches mark mainly Christmas and Easter.

games.q: it's the first Sunday of Advent, in late November. after church a friend says, happy new year! what does she mean?
games.why: in the Western churches, the liturgical year begins on the first Sunday of Advent, and the circle starts again with waiting.

practice: Picture the seasons going round: waiting, birth, light, desert, cross, empty tomb, fire, and the long green ordinary.
Never mind today's date; ask which season your own life feels like this month: waiting for something, in a desert, or somewhere ordinary and green.
If you pray, bring that season to God as it is; if you don't, just name it and sit with it.

wordCard.voice: Liturgical year. The church's calendar of seasons and colors, walking through the life of Christ every year. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: a public work or service. the root of liturgy.

carryVoice: Your line: time can be holy. Purple, white, green, red: the clock keeps turning. That's day one hundred nine.
